messages.author: bd1e86fc1630832f
messages.subject: Multivariate Hierarchical Bayesian Modeling
parts:
In a couple of projects now, I have wanted to estimate multiple hyper-parameters in an hierarchical Bayesian model, accounting for the covariance between parameters as reported by each component study.

So, the model is:
  y_i ~ N(theta_i, Sigma_i)  (where y_i is a vector of estimated parameters from study i, and Sigma_i is the estimated VCV matrix).
  theta_i ~ N(mu, Tau)
where theta_i is the Bayesian-estimated "true" study parameter, mu is a vector and Tau is a VCV matrix (also Bayesian-estimated).

When I estimate each parameter independently, using a normal hierarchical Bayesian model, everything works beautifully.
When I try to estimate the model above using Stan, as soon as I have more than about 10 observations, the sampler seems to be unable to explore the distribution (each chain just gets a separate, tightly estimated set of parameters), and my n_eff = #chains / 2.  This is true, despite trying to do this with very different datasets.

I have tried a number of ways of writing this model, and I've tried normalizing the scale of parameters so that they are all similar.  Any ideas?

Below are two versions of the model, where I either estimate a full VCV matrix for Tau or where I do not allow covariance in Tau.

Model 1 (as above):
data {
    int<lower=1> N; // number of study regions
    int<lower=1> K; // number of coefficients

    vector[K] beta[N]; // estimated effects
    cov_matrix[K] Sigma[N]; // VCV across betas
}
transformed data {
    // Optimization: only compute decomposition once
    matrix[K, K] CholL[N];
    for (ii in 1:N)
      CholL[ii] = cholesky_decompose(Sigma[ii]);
}
parameters {
    vector[K] mu; // hyper parameters
    cov_matrix[K] Tau; // variance in hyper equation
    vector[K] theta[N]; // z-scores of true effects
}
model {
    // observed betas drawn from true parameters
    for (ii in 1:N) {
       beta[ii] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(theta[ii], CholL[ii]);
       theta[ii] ~ multi_normal(mu, Tau);
    }
}

Model 2 (simplified Tau):
data {
    int<lower=1> N; // number of study regions
    int<lower=1> K; // number of coefficients

    vector[K] beta[N]; // estimated effects
    cov_matrix[K] Sigma[N]; // VCV across betas
}
transformed data {
    // Optimization: only compute decomposition once
    matrix[K, K] CholL[N];
    for (ii in 1:N)
      CholL[ii] = cholesky_decompose(Sigma[ii]);
}
parameters {
    real mu[K]; // hyper parameters
    real<lower=0> tau[K]; // variance in hyper equation
    vector[K] theta[N]; // z-scores of true effects
}
transformed parameters {
    vector[N] transtheta[K]; // transpose of theta
    for (ii in 1:N) {
      for (kk in 1:K)
        transtheta[kk][ii] = theta[ii][kk];
    }
}
model {
    // observed betas drawn from true parameters
    for (ii in 1:N)
       beta[ii] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(theta[ii], CholL[ii]);

    // true parameters produced by linear expression
    for (kk in 1:K) {
      target += normal_lpdf(transtheta[kk] | mu[kk], tau[kk]);
    }
}

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Multivariate Hierarchical Bayesian Modeling
parts:
Two things you'll probably need to do:

1. Switch to a Cholesky-factor parameterization of Tau
with a proper prior. We recommend the scaled correlation
matrix version as outlined in the regression chapter
of the manual. The prior will help avoid extreme values and
the parameterization will be more stable arithmetically.

2. Switch to a non-centered parameterization. That's harder
in the multivariate case (see the efficiency chapter on
reparameterization under "Multivariate Reparameterizations").

You can also vectorize this whole thing, which will be a lot
faster. See the chapter on efficiency in the manual.

- Bob
